problem: Human cognition faces fundamental processing limitations and working memory constraints that create a gap between perception and reasoning, often leading to cognitive overload and decision-making biases (p.1, p.2). Existing LLMs are predominantly reactive and lack contextual awareness, providing one-size-fits-all responses rather than adapting to users' cognitive processes and task environments (p.1, p.2, p.5).
methodology: The authors conducted a preliminary think-aloud study in an exhibition setting where three MPhil or PhD students navigated exhibits, captured and synthesized information for a report, and verbalized their thoughts, strategies, and challenges (p.3, p.4). Interactions were recorded via video, followed by semi-structured interviews to capture reflections on their experience and expectations for AI-driven cognitive support (p.4).
dataset: The study recruited three participants who were MPhil or PhD students from the university, each with at least five years of experience in design or development (p.4).
results: Findings reveal that participants experienced challenges in structuring contextual information, retrieving knowledge, and leveraging digital tools for context-aware, structured, and proactive engagement (p.2). Participants processed information across multiple modalities (text, video, interactive displays, and physical gestures) but struggled with organizing and retrieving captured photographs and personal notes (p.4, p.5).
key_findings: Participants adjusted their engagement strategies based on environmental and social constraints, hesitating to use real-time verbal commentary or overt gestures due to privacy and public discretion (p.5). Participants demonstrated diverse cognitive workflows, with some constructing broad conceptual frameworks first and others adopting a detail-oriented approach before synthesizing insights (p.5).
title: Intelligent Interaction Strategies for Context-Aware Cognitive Augmentation
